title: Measuring Enzyme Activity: Units, NADH at 340 nm and the LD Direction
summary: Learn what an enzyme unit and a katal are and how to convert between them, why NADH at 340 nm is the signal behind common enzyme assays such as ALT and LD, why activity is read from the initial rate with a fixed dilution, and why the IFCC LD method runs from lactate to pyruvate.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 21 Hits 7 (U and katal), 8 (NADH at 340 nm) and 9 (dilution and initial velocity) and Trap 4 (LD reaction direction). Units from the BIPM SI Brochure (CGPM 1999 Resolution 12); measurand-by-procedure from Infusino 2009 and Siekmann 2001; NADH coefficient and the coupled ALT assay from Sun 2021 and Hu 2026; initial velocity from Robinson 2015 and Rendón 2025; dilution from Ramsay 2017 and Jońca 2015; LD direction from the IFCC LD method (Bais 1994; abstract read via a page-fetch tool, full-text PDF blocked by a captcha) and Voma 2016 (read via a page-fetch tool). The reviewer gives “specificity” as the reason the forward LD reaction is preferred; the IFCC method states linearity, a rising absorbance and substrate optimisation (register flag rv-ld-direction-rationale). The reviewer’s “most enzyme assays are secretly NADH assays” is softened to “several common assays, such as ALT and LD”. Not taught: Hit 13 temperature rule (doubling per 10 °C, ±0.1 °C), which no open source read in this session supported (IFCC 37 °C papers in Clin Chem Lab Med were not accessible); Hit 14 catalytic perfection; the Number Vault table.

objectives: Define the enzyme unit and the katal and convert between U/L and µkat/L.
Explain why NADH at 340 nm (ε 6.22 × 10³ L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹) is the signal in direct and coupled enzyme assays.
Explain why activity is read from the initial rate, how dilution affects reversible inhibitors, and why the IFCC LD method runs lactate → pyruvate.

scenes.title: Same enzyme, three different numbers
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three puzzles about one serum enzyme reach the chemistry bench — (1) a referral report gives LD in µkat/L while the local report uses U/L; (2) a colleague proposes an LD kit that runs pyruvate → lactate “because it gives higher, faster readings”; (3) a cholinesterase activity rises when the same serum is diluted more before assay. Question token: “Same enzyme, different numbers: why?”

cues.text: Three puzzles about enzyme numbers reach the chemistry bench. A referral report gives LD in microkatals per litre, while the local report uses units per litre.
A colleague wants an LD kit that runs pyruvate to lactate, because it gives higher readings. And a cholinesterase result rises when the serum is diluted more.
Same enzyme, different numbers. Why?

scenes.title: Activity is a rate under stated conditions
scenes.altText: Units card (BIPM SI Brochure, CGPM 1999 Resolution 12): the “unit”, U, equals 1 µmol of substrate converted per minute and has been used in medicine since 1964; the coherent SI unit is the katal, kat = 1 mol per second. Conversion card (arithmetic from the definitions): 1 U = 10⁻⁶ mol ÷ 60 s ≈ 16.7 nkat; 1 kat = 6 × 10⁷ U; so U/L × 0.0167 = µkat/L. Conditions card: catalytic activity is a measured rate, not an amount of substance; change pH, buffer, temperature, substrate, activators or inhibitors and the number changes. The IFCC reference procedures (now at 37 °C, rebuilt from the 30 °C methods) define the measurand, including the reaction direction, temperature, lag phase, measurement time and wavelength. The CGPM recommends that whenever the katal is used the measurement procedure, including the indicator reaction, be specified.

cues.text: Enzymes are not counted; their activity is measured as a rate. The classic unit, U, is one micromole of substrate converted per minute.
The SI unit is the katal: one mole per second. So one U is about sixteen point seven nanokatals, and one katal is sixty million U.
The number depends on the conditions. Change the pH, buffer, temperature, substrate or inhibitors, and the activity changes. That is why the result must name its method.
IFCC reference procedures, now run at thirty-seven degrees, fix those conditions, including the reaction direction and the wavelength.

props.label: IFCC reference: 37 °C, direction and wavelength fixed

scenes.title: Reading NADH at 340 nm
scenes.altText: Spectrum card (schematic): NADH absorbs strongly at 340 nm; NAD⁺ absorbs very little there. Coefficient card: molar absorption coefficient of NADH at 340 nm = 6.22 × 10³ L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹ (6.22 cm²/µmol). Coupled card (ALT example): ALT turns alanine into pyruvate; an added lactate dehydrogenase reduces that pyruvate to lactate while oxidising NADH to NAD⁺, so absorbance at 340 nm falls at a rate proportional to ALT activity. Direct card (LD, lactate → pyruvate): NAD⁺ → NADH, so absorbance at 340 nm rises. Calculation card: the rate of absorbance change, divided by the coefficient (and the light path), gives micromoles of NADH per minute.

cues.text: Several common enzyme assays, such as ALT and LD, are read through one molecule: NADH. NADH absorbs strongly at three hundred and forty nanometres, while NAD plus absorbs very little there.
Its molar absorption coefficient at that wavelength is six point two two times ten to the third litres per mole per centimetre.
Coupling links other enzymes to this signal. In the ALT assay, ALT makes pyruvate, and an added lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to turn it into lactate. The fall in absorbance tracks ALT activity.
In the LD assay run from lactate to pyruvate, NADH is made, so absorbance rises. Either way, the rate of change divided by the coefficient gives micromoles per minute.

scenes.title: Initial rate, dilution and the LD direction
scenes.altText: Progress-curve card (schematic): product formation is linear at first, then slows because substrate is used up, product accumulates and may inhibit, the reverse reaction grows, or the enzyme loses activity — so activity is taken from the initial linear rate. Dilution card: reversible inhibition can be reversed by dilution (or dialysis); irreversible inhibition cannot. In one butyrylcholinesterase study, serum contained an inhibitory factor (larger than 3 kDa), and measured activity rose with the dilution factor, so the dilution must be standardised. LD-direction card: either direction can be measured; the reverse (pyruvate → lactate) reaction can run 2–3 times faster, but the IFCC chose lactate → pyruvate because its time course is more linear, absorbance increases, and substrates could be optimised; pyruvate can also be used by other enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase. Hook answers.

cues.text: Watch a reaction over time. It starts straight, then bends: substrate runs out, product builds up and may inhibit, and the reverse reaction grows. So activity is read from the initial straight part.

Dilution helps with reversible inhibitors. In one cholinesterase study, serum held an inhibitory factor, and measured activity rose as the serum was diluted more, so the dilution must be standardised.

LD can be measured either way. Pyruvate to lactate can run two to three times faster, but the IFCC chose lactate to pyruvate: a more linear time course, a rising absorbance, and substrates that could be optimised.
Back to the hook. Convert units with the definitions, keep the lactate to pyruvate method, and dilute by a fixed, stated factor.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The faster pyruvate → lactate LD reaction is the reference method” (✓ IFCC uses lactate → pyruvate: more linear, absorbance rises; pyruvate can be used by other enzymes); “1 U equals 1 katal” (✓ 1 U = 1 µmol/min ≈ 16.7 nkat; 1 kat = 6 × 10⁷ U); “NAD⁺ is what is read at 340 nm” (✓ NADH absorbs at 340 nm; NAD⁺ absorbs very little).

cues.text: Trap one: the faster pyruvate to lactate reaction is the reference LD method. No: the IFCC runs lactate to pyruvate, which is more linear and gives a rising absorbance.
Trap two: one unit equals one katal. No: a unit is a micromole per minute, about sixteen point seven nanokatals.
Trap three: NAD plus is what is read at three hundred and forty nanometres. No: NADH absorbs there; NAD plus barely does.

And LD’s reference road starts at Lactate: L before P, like the alphabet.” Tokens: µmol/min vs mol/s · 6.22 at 340 · L → P. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the U is a micromole per minute, the katal a whole mole per second, sixty million apart. NADH carries a passport stamped six point two two at the three-forty gate. And the reference LD road starts at lactate: L before P, like the alphabet.
Where it breaks: activity numbers compare only when the procedure is the same; not every enzyme assay uses NADH; and dilution helps only with reversible inhibitors, not irreversible ones.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Activity = rate under stated conditions · 1 U = 1 µmol/min ≈ 16.7 nkat · 1 kat = 1 mol/s”, “NADH at 340 nm (ε 6.22 × 10³) · initial rate · fixed dilution · IFCC LD: lactate → pyruvate”.

cues.text: Enzyme activity is a rate under stated conditions, reported as micromoles per minute or as katals of one mole per second, often read through NADH at 340 nm from the initial straight part of the curve, and the reference LD method runs from lactate to pyruvate.

props.label: Rate under stated conditions · 1 U = 1 µmol/min ≈ 16.7 nkat
NADH at 340 nm · initial rate · fixed dilution · LD: L → P

explanation.what: Plain language: an enzyme result is not a count of enzyme molecules but how fast the enzyme works in a test tube under fixed conditions. Labs usually watch a molecule called NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm, appear or disappear. Scientific terms: catalytic activity, enzyme unit (U, µmol/min), katal (kat, mol/s), catalytic concentration (U/L, µkat/L), reference measurement procedure, NADH/NAD⁺, molar absorption coefficient, coupled (indicator) reaction, initial velocity (v₀), progress curve, reversible inhibition, reaction direction.
explanation.why: Because activity is a rate, its value depends on pH, buffer, temperature, substrate and the reaction measured. Fixing these in a reference procedure, reading the early linear part of the reaction, and controlling dilution make results comparable. NADH gives a convenient optical signal because NAD⁺ hardly absorbs at 340 nm.
explanation.measure: 1 U = 1 µmol/min; 1 kat = 1 mol/s; 1 U ≈ 16.7 nkat; 1 kat = 6 × 10⁷ U; U/L × 0.0167 = µkat/L. NADH ε at 340 nm = 6.22 × 10³ L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹ (6.22 cm²/µmol). ALT: coupled with lactate dehydrogenase, A340 falls. LD (IFCC): lactate → pyruvate, A340 rises; the reverse reaction can be 2–3 times faster.
explanation.differs: U vs katal; NADH (absorbs at 340 nm) vs NAD⁺ (barely absorbs); direct vs coupled assay; initial rate vs later slowed rate; reversible (dilution reverses) vs irreversible inhibition; lactate → pyruvate (IFCC reference) vs pyruvate → lactate (faster, not the reference).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: convert nkat/L or µkat/L to U/L, recall the NADH wavelength and coefficient, predict whether absorbance rises or falls, choose the LD reaction direction used by the IFCC, or explain why initial velocity is measured.

takeaway: Enzyme activity is a rate under stated conditions, reported as micromoles per minute or as katals of one mole per second, often read through NADH at 340 nm from the initial straight part of the curve, and the reference LD method runs from lactate to pyruvate.

questions.stem: A referral laboratory reports an enzyme as 0.50 µkat/L. Approximately what is this in U/L (1 U = 1 µmol/min)?

options.rationale: Correct. 1 µkat = 1 µmol/s = 60 µmol/min = 60 U, so 0.50 µkat/L ≈ 30 U/L.
Incorrect. A katal is a mole per second, not a micromole per minute; the units are not equal.
Incorrect. This multiplies by 16.7, the nanokatal-per-U factor; to go from µkat/L to U/L, multiply by 60.
Incorrect. This treats micro as milli; 1 µkat equals 60 U, not 60 000 U.

questions.stem: In a coupled ALT assay, ALT makes pyruvate and an added lactate dehydrogenase converts it to lactate. What is monitored, and in which direction does it change?

options.text: Absorbance at 340 nm falls as NADH is oxidised to NAD⁺
options.rationale: Correct. NADH absorbs at 340 nm and NAD⁺ barely does, so the absorbance falls at a rate proportional to ALT activity.

options.text: Absorbance at 340 nm rises as NAD⁺ is formed
options.rationale: Incorrect. NAD⁺ absorbs very little at 340 nm; forming it lowers the absorbance.

options.text: Absorbance at 260 nm rises as pyruvate accumulates
options.rationale: Incorrect. The indicator is NADH at 340 nm, not pyruvate.

options.text: The final lactate concentration after the reaction stops
options.rationale: Incorrect. Activity is a rate, taken from the change in absorbance per minute.

questions.stem: Why does the IFCC method measure lactate dehydrogenase in the lactate → pyruvate direction, even though the reverse reaction can run 2–3 times faster?

options.text: Its time course is more linear and the absorbance at 340 nm increases
options.rationale: Correct. These are among the reasons the IFCC LD method (Bais 1994) gives, along with the ability to optimise substrates.

options.text: Only the forward reaction produces a change at 340 nm
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both directions change NADH; the reverse reaction lowers the absorbance.

options.text: The faster a reaction, the less accurate it is by definition
options.rationale: Incorrect. Speed alone is not the reason; linearity and defined conditions are.

options.text: Pyruvate cannot be used as an LD substrate
options.rationale: Incorrect. LD catalyses a reversible reaction, and either direction can be measured.

claims.text: U = 1 µmol/min; katal = 1 mol/s; 1 U ≈ 16.7 nkat; 1 kat = 6 × 10⁷ U; procedure must be specified.
Activity is a rate that depends on conditions; IFCC reference procedures at 37 °C define direction, temperature and wavelength.
NADH absorbs at 340 nm, NAD⁺ barely does; ε = 6.22 × 10³ L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹; activity from ΔA/min using ε.
Coupled ALT assay: lactate dehydrogenase oxidises NADH; A340 falls in proportion to ALT activity. LD (L → P) forms NADH, A340 rises.
Initial velocity measured because the rate later falls (substrate depletion, product inhibition, reverse reaction, enzyme instability).
Dilution reverses reversible but not irreversible inhibition; serum inhibitory factor made BChE activity rise with dilution.
IFCC LD method uses lactate → pyruvate (more linear, absorbance rises, substrates optimisable); the reverse can be 2–3 times faster; pyruvate also used by other enzymes.
Reviewer Hit 13: activity roughly doubles per 10 °C and reaction temperature must stay within ±0.1 °C. Not taught; no open source read in this session supported the figures.
Reviewer: “most enzyme assays are secretly NADH assays”. Taught only as “several common assays, such as ALT and LD”; no source read gives a proportion.
Scenario invented; spectrum and progress curve schematic.
“Minute versus second, 6.22 at 340, L before P.”

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says the forward (lactate → pyruvate) LD reaction is preferred “for specificity” because pyruvate is attacked by other enzymes. The IFCC LD method states its reasons as a more linear time course, a rising absorbance and substrate optimisation; an ADLM teaching source lists pyruvate use by pyruvate dehydrogenase as one of several reasons, alongside IFCC-defined conditions, lactate being the preferred LD substrate and possible underestimation by the reverse reaction. The lesson teaches the IFCC reasons and mentions the pyruvate side reaction only as a supporting point.

Hit 13’s temperature rule (doubling per 10 °C; ±0.1 °C tolerance) could not be checked against an accessible open source in this session (IFCC 37 °C procedures in Clin Chem Lab Med and Franzini 1988 full text were not readable), so it is not taught here.

morphology.note: No images; spectrum, reactions and progress curve shown as schematic cards.
